papers.title: Cross-domain competition for memory reactivation resources during sleep
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768209 v1

summary.one_liner: In a within-subject nap study (n=24), cueing object-task memories during NREM sleep with targeted memory reactivation did not indirectly strengthen a linked motor memory, and sleep EEG slow oscillation and spindle activity appeared to favor the motor trace over the object memory.
summary.plain: When we learn two related skills, our brains may replay memories of them during sleep, and the two can end up competing. This study used sound or scent-style cues tied to one task during a 90-minute nap to see whether replaying an object-task memory would also replay a linked motor-task memory. The object memory got worse rather than better, and brain-wave patterns suggested the motor memory received the sleep processing instead.
summary.why: It suggests memories that share a common structure may compete for limited sleep-time consolidation resources, which matters for how we design memory-boosting sleep interventions. The text does not establish how general this competition is or whether it holds beyond this task pairing, so the finding should be treated as preliminary.
summary.background:
- Targeted memory reactivation (TMR): pairing a cue (often a sound) learned during waking practice with that memory, then presenting the cue again during sleep to reactivate it.
- NREM sleep: the deeper, non-dream sleep stages where memory consolidation is thought to occur.
- Slow oscillations (0.5-2 Hz) and sleep spindles (12-16 Hz): rhythms in sleep EEG (brain electrical recordings) thought to help move and protect memories.
- Declarative vs. procedural memory: facts/events versus learned motor or skill sequences.
- Within-subject design: each participant does all conditions, so comparisons are made within the same people.
- Covert consolidation: memory processing that happens without a behavioral change being directly visible.

papers.abstract: Targeted Memory Reactivation (TMR) enhances the consolidation of both declarative and procedural memories. As previous research highlights the importance of cross-domain interactions in shaping memory consolidation, we investigated here whether interacting memories from different domains can be co-reactivated by TMR during post-learning sleep, and in turn enhance consolidation. In a fully within-subject design, twenty-four young, healthy participants learned both a motor and an object sequence learning task that were linked or not by a shared ordinal structure. TMR cues associated only with the object task were presented during post-learning non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep which was monitored with electroencephalography (EEG) during a 90-minute nap. We tested whether reactivating object memories would indirectly reactivate the linked motor memory. Behavioral results showed no overall effect of association but indicated that TMR disrupted object memory consolidation without indirectly affecting performance on the linked motor task. Sleep EEG data point to a competition for reactivation resources whereby slow oscillation (SO; 0.5-2 Hz) and spindle activity (12-16 Hz) involved in both memory protection and potentiation during sleep were preferentially allocated to the covert consolidation of the motor trace at the expense of object memory. These findings suggest that cross-domain memories sharing a common learning structure compete for consolidation resources during post-learning sleep.

papers.title: Reduced bushy cell firing limits binaural coding after cochlear synaptopathy
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.768331 v1

summary.one_liner: A computational model of the auditory brainstem tests how cochlear synaptopathy (loss of auditory nerve inputs to bushy cells) and increased temporal jitter in bushy cell outputs, modeled as central myelin dysfunction, each impair binaural coding in the lateral superior olive.
summary.plain: People can have trouble hearing in noisy settings and locating sounds even when their standard hearing tests look normal. This paper uses a computer model of the hearing pathway to test two possible causes: losing some of the nerve connections from the ear, and nerve signals that arrive with less precise timing. The model found that each cause reduces the brain's ability to compare the two ears' signals, but in different ways.
summary.why: It offers a mechanistic account of how hidden hearing damage could affect spatial hearing and speech in noise, which may matter for people with normal audiograms. The text is a model-based study, so its predictions about real listeners are not tested here, and the link to human hearing difficulties remains a hypothesis.
summary.background:
- Cochlear synaptopathy: loss of connections between inner hair cells in the ear and auditory nerve fibers, which can occur without raising the hearing threshold.
- Bushy cells: neurons in the cochlear nucleus (first brainstem hearing station) that receive auditory nerve input and relay timing information.
- Lateral superior olive (LSO): a brainstem site that compares loudness between the two ears, helping locate sounds.
- Interaural envelope phase differences: small timing differences in the loudness fluctuations of a sound reaching each ear, used for spatial hearing.
- Phase locking: how precisely a neuron's spikes follow the timing of a sound wave.
- Temporal jitter: random variation in spike timing, here used to model myelin-related transmission problems.
- Computational model: a simulation built from physiological data, not a study with human or animal recordings in this text.

papers.abstract: Listeners can experience difficulties with spatial hearing and speech understanding in complex acoustic environments despite near-normal hearing thresholds. Cochlear synaptopathy, which reduces auditory nerve input without elevating thresholds, is one candidate mechanism, but how this peripheral deafferentation disrupts binaural processing remains unclear. We adapted a physiologically constrained computational model incorporating the auditory periphery, spherical and globular bushy cells of the cochlear nucleus and the lateral superior olive (LSO) to examine the separate and combined effects of reduced afferent input and degraded spike timing. Synaptopathy was modeled as loss of auditory nerve inputs to bushy cells, whereas central myelin dysfunction was modeled as increased temporal jitter in bushy cell outputs. Loss of auditory nerve input substantially reduced bushy cell firing rates without degrading phase locking. Despite this preserved temporal precision, binaural tuning in the LSO declined disproportionately, where moderate afferent loss produced substantial reductions in sensitivity to interaural envelope phase differences. In contrast, temporal jitter preserved bushy cell firing rates but degraded phase locking and binaural tuning. Selective loss of input to excitatory versus inhibitory pathways produced opposite changes in overall LSO firing rate, yet both reduced binaural interaction. These results identify two mechanistically distinct routes to impaired binaural coding: too few precisely timed spikes, and a sufficient number of spikes arriving with inadequate temporal precision. These results predict that correcting myelin-related timing deficits alone would leave substantial binaural coding impairment when cochlear deafferentation persists, motivating interventions that address both diminished afferent drive and impaired transmission.

papers.title: Sex-dependent gating of astrocyte-driven nociceptive plasticity
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767473 v1

summary.background:
- Synaptic plasticity: lasting strengthening or weakening of connections between nerve cells; it is one proposed basis for learning and for pain that persists.
- Nociception: the nervous system's detection and signaling of potentially harmful stimuli.
- Astrocytes: star-shaped support cells in the nervous system that also influence nearby synapses.
- G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): cell-surface receptors that trigger internal signaling; chemogenetics uses engineered versions to switch specific cells on or off with a drug.
- Gonadectomy / ovariectomy and testosterone treatment: surgical removal of sex glands and hormone replacement, used to test hormone effects.
- Perineuronal nets: mesh-like extracellular matrix structures around neurons that can limit how easily connections change.
- Mechanical hypersensitivity: increased pain response to light touch or pressure, typically measured in animals with filaments.
summary.one_liner: In rats, chemogenetic activation of distinct spinal astrocyte GPCR pathways produced synaptic depression or potentiation at nociceptive synapses in males but not females, and the female-specific gating was linked to hormonal status and extracellular matrix organization.
summary.plain: This study looks at how support cells in the spinal cord, called astrocytes, can change how strongly pain signals pass between nerve cells, and whether that effect differs between male and female rats. The researchers activated astrocytes with engineered receptors and found that this changed pain-signal connections in males but not in females. Still, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity (heightened sensitivity to touch) about as much as males, so the change in connections and the change in pain behavior did not track each other.
summary.why: Sex differences in pain are well documented but their cellular basis is poorly understood, and this paper points to hormones and the brain's extracellular matrix as possible switches controlling whether astrocytes can reshape pain circuits. The finding that synaptic plasticity and pain behavior can dissociate is worth noting, though the text alone does not show how this relates to chronic pain in people.

papers.abstract: Sex differences in pain are well established, yet how nociceptive processing is differentially regulated across sexes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that spinal astrocytes provide pathway-specific control of acute nociceptive synaptic plasticity in rats. Chemogenetic activation of distinct astrocytic G-protein-coupled receptor pathways induced synaptic depression or potentiation at spinal nociceptive synapses in males, but failed to evoke detectable plasticity in females. Despite this lack of astrocyte-induced synaptic plasticity, females developed mechanical hypersensitivity comparable to males, revealing a dissociation between synaptic plasticity and pain-related behavior. Gonadectomy prevented astrocyte-induced plasticity in males, whereas testosterone treatment enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in ovariectomized females. Females exhibited more prominent perineuronal net labeling, and enzymatic degradation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components enabled Gq-dependent synaptic depression in females. Together, these findings identify hormonal status and ECM organization as important determinants of the susceptibility of spinal nociceptive circuits to astrocyte-driven synaptic plasticity.

papers.title: Concurrent neuronal activity gates persistent dendritic spine shrinkage during mGluR-induced long-term depression
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.21.765465 v1

summary.background:
- Synapses: junctions where one neuron passes signals to another; most excitatory ones sit on dendritic spines.
- LTP / LTD: long-lasting strengthening / weakening of a synapse, thought to underlie learning and memory.
- Structural vs functional plasticity: changes in spine size and shape versus changes in signal strength.
- mGluR and NMDAR: two types of glutamate receptors (the brain's main excitatory chemical messenger); DHPG is a chemical that activates mGluR1/5.
- Organotypic slice culture: a thin slice of brain tissue kept alive in a dish.
- GCaMP6 and DsRed2: fluorescent markers used to track calcium activity and spine structure.
- Two-photon glutamate uncaging: a laser-based way to release glutamate onto a single spine.
- Coincidence detection: a process that responds only when two inputs arrive together.
summary.one_liner: In organotypic rat hippocampal slices, mGluR1/5-induced LTD produced persistent dendritic spine shrinkage only when neuronal activity coincided with mGluR activation, a process the authors call MIND-sLTD that depends on mGluR1/5 and protein synthesis but not NMDARs.
summary.plain: Brain cells connect at small bumps called dendritic spines, and when a connection weakens, its spine tends to shrink. This paper asks whether shrinkage also happens when the weakening is triggered by a different receptor type (metabotropic glutamate receptors), where earlier reports disagreed. The authors chemically activated these receptors in slices of rat brain tissue and watched individual spines and calcium signals under a microscope. They found lasting shrinkage only when the cells were also firing actively at the same time.
summary.why: The work offers a possible explanation for conflicting earlier reports by suggesting that timing with neural activity matters for whether spines stay smaller. It may matter for understanding how memories are structurally consolidated, but the text alone does not establish how general or behaviorally relevant the effect is.

papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity is a fundamental mechanism underlying learning and memory. Most excitatory synapses reside on dendritic spines, which undergo both functional and structural changes. These two forms of plasticity are typically tightly coupled: spines enlarge during synaptic strengthening (long-term potentiation, LTP) and shrink during synaptic weakening (long-term depression, LTD). While this coupling is well established for NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent LTD, there are conflicting reports concerning whether spine shrinkage is coupled with metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD. To investigate the source of these conflicting results, we induced mGluR-LTD with the mGluR1/5 agonist DHPG in organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures and monitored changes in spine morphology and calcium transients in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing DsRed2 and GCaMP6. We found that mGluR activation is accompanied by long-term spine shrinkage only under conditions of elevated hippocampal neuronal activity. This form of plasticity, mGluR-induced neuronal activity-dependent structural LTD (MIND-sLTD), requires mGluR1/5 activation and de novo protein synthesis, but not NMDAR signaling. Persistent structural changes occur only when neuronal activity coincides temporally with mGluR activation. MIND-sLTD also occurs at individual synapses: mGluR activation induces persistent single-spine shrinkage only when synchronized with two-photon glutamate uncaging, independently of NMDARs. These findings identify a novel form of structural plasticity and suggest a coincidence-detection mechanism that integrates mGluR signaling with synaptic activity to consolidate long-term spine remodeling.

papers.title: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D regulates hippocampal memory through extracellular matrix remodeling
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768232 v1

summary.background:
- Astrocytes: star-shaped glial cells that support neurons and release signaling molecules.
- Hippocampus: a brain region essential for forming new memories.
- Long-term potentiation (LTP): a lasting strengthening of connections between neurons, widely used as a cellular model of learning.
- Extracellular matrix (ECM): the mesh of sugar-protein molecules outside cells that helps hold tissue structure and regulates synapses.
- Cathepsin D: an enzyme that usually breaks down proteins, here studied for a role outside cells.
- Chondroitinase ABC: an enzyme that cuts down certain ECM sugar chains, used here as a tool to test the matrix's role.
- Knockdown: reducing how much of a gene's product a cell makes.
summary.one_liner: Astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D is reported to shape hippocampal LTP and memory acquisition in mice, apparently by remodeling the extracellular matrix around synapses.
summary.plain: Brain support cells called astrocytes release proteins that may influence how memories form. This study focuses on one such protein, Cathepsin D, which is normally known for breaking down material inside cells. The authors found that blocking it outside astrocytes, or knocking it down in astrocytes of mice, weakened a measure of synaptic strengthening (LTP) and impaired memory acquisition, and that partially digesting a surrounding matrix material restored memory in these mice.
summary.why: It points to a possible link between astrocytes, the extracellular matrix that surrounds neurons, and synapse strength in memory, a mechanism that has received less attention than neuron-to-neuron signaling. The text does not establish how broadly these findings apply beyond the mouse experiments described.

papers.abstract: Astrocytes contribute to hippocampal cognitive functions, but how astrocyte-derived factors regulate memory formation remains unclear. Here, we identify astrocyte-secreted Cathepsin D (CtsD) as a regulator of hippocampal learning and memory. Proteomic profiling of hippocampal astrocytes upon learning identified candidates predicted to be secreted, among which we focused on CtsD, whose extracellular brain functions are unknown. Neutralizing extracellular CtsD or astrocyte-selective CtsD knockdown (aCtsD-KD) impaired hippocampal long term potentiation (LTP) and memory acquisition, suggesting an extracellular role for astrocytic CtsD. In aCtsD-KD mice, these deficits were accompanied by alterations in excitatory transmission and synaptic structures. aCtsD-KD also caused abnormal extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation, and its partial digestion by chondroitinase ABC rescued the memory deficit, indicating that astrocytic CtsD-dependent ECM degradation contributes to hippocampal memory. Together, our findings suggest a CtsD-dependent astrocyte-matrix-synapse axis regulating hippocampal memory.

papers.title: Unexpected Long Range Actions of AAV8
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.767967 v1

summary.background:
- AAV (adeno-associated virus) is a harmless, engineered virus used to deliver genes into specific cells.
- Titer is the concentration of virus particles in an injection; higher titer usually means more cells are infected.
- Capsid is the protein shell around the virus that influences which cells it infects and how it spreads.
- Recombinase (such as Cre) is an enzyme that cuts and rearranges DNA in engineered cells; a reporter then reveals which cells had that activity.
- Starter population means the cells directly infected by the injection.
- Monosynaptic means a direct, single-step connection between two neurons; tracing methods aim to label only these.
- The corticopontocerebellar tract is a brain pathway running from the cortex through the pons to the cerebellum, used here as a test system.
summary.one_liner: In mice, high-titer AAV8 injected into the corticopontocerebellar pathway produced recombination outside the injected starter cells, depending on titer and on other co-injections, including across regions not known to be monosynaptically connected.
summary.plain: Researchers use harmless viruses to carry genetic tools into brain cells, and they often assume the virus only affects the cells it was injected into. This paper reports that a common virus type, AAV8, given at high concentration, can switch on genetic reporters in distant cells that were not directly infected. The effect depended on the dose and on what other virus injections were made at the same time.
summary.why: This matters for anyone who uses viral tools to map brain circuits, because labeled cells far from the injection site could be mistaken for directly connected cells. The text suggests that the effect may come from spread beyond the starter cells, but the mechanism is not established here.

papers.abstract: Adeno-associated virus vectors (AAVs) have broad utility in neuroscience. A variety of features, such as titer, capsid, enhancers and promoters, coding and non-coding elements, can be utilized to pursue diverse experimental ends. The net effects of titer and capsid have been used experimentally to pursue retrograde and anterograde studies, such as through the monosynaptic spread of high-titer AAV1. The literature on AAV8 is conflicting, with evidence for and against its long-range action outside of the infected starter population. Using the mouse corticopontocerebellar tract, we report that AAV8, when used at high titers, can be associated with long range recombination outside of the starter population. This phenomenon depended upon the viral titer and was influenced by the presence of other experimental injections. Surprisingly, separate injections of high-titer AAV8 recombinase and recombinase-reporter AAV8s gave rise to recombination across long distances in populations not known to be monosynaptically connected. Given the possibility of long range and emergent effects, we suggest that investigators empirically determine titer, capsid, and injection designs that reduce false positives and/or indirect effects.

papers.title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767959 v1

summary.background:
- Spike sorting: separating the electrical spikes recorded on one electrode into the individual neurons that produced them.
- Multiunit activity: the combined spike signal from many neurons, without separating them.
- Population trajectories: paths traced through a high-dimensional space by the activity of many neurons over time, often reduced to a few dimensions.
- Intrinsic timescale: how quickly a neuron's activity fluctuations decay over time.
- Neurometric threshold: the smallest stimulus difference an ensemble of neural responses can reliably detect.
- UMAP and HDBSCAN: computational tools for grouping spike waveforms into clusters.
- Decoding: predicting what a subject is doing or perceiving from recorded brain activity.
summary.one_liner: Compares nonlinear (UMAP/HDBSCAN) spike sorting, linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit threshold crossings from the same monkey recordings in somatosensory and premotor cortex, asking which analyses need single-neuron identity.
summary.plain: Brain recordings pick up electrical spikes from many nearby nerve cells mixed together, and researchers must decide whether to separate them into individual neurons or just use the combined signal. Using previously published data from four monkeys, the authors built three versions of the same spikes and compared them. They found that the combined signal is good enough for analyses of the shared overall pattern of activity, such as decoding, but separating individual neurons was needed for measures like timing, variability and how neurons individually encode information.

papers.abstract: Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. Using previously published recordings from four rhesus monkeys, we analyzed areas 3b and 1 of primary somatosensory cortex and ventral premotor cortex during a bimodal detection task, and ventral premotor cortex during an interval comparison task. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.

papers.title: Motor learning engages intrinsic plasticity in the human cortex
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767269 v1

summary.background:
- Synaptic strength: how strongly one neuron influences another; the usual explanation for learning.
- Intrinsic excitability/plasticity: how readily a neuron itself turns incoming signals into firing; changes here are seen in animals.
- Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS): a coil over the scalp that briefly stimulates the brain; the motor-evoked potential (MEP) is the muscle twitch it produces and is mainly a measure of synaptic excitability.
- Controllable-pulse TMS: a TMS variant that shapes the pulse, allowing indirect estimates of neuron-level properties.
- Motor cortex representation: the brain area controlling a given muscle; the trained muscle was compared with an untrained one as a control.
- Axon model: a computer simulation of a nerve fibre, used here to check whether small membrane changes could explain the measurements.
summary.one_liner: Using controllable-pulse TMS to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, the paper reports training-related increases specific to the trained muscle's representation, with larger intrinsic changes linked to faster learning independent of synaptic-type MEP changes.
summary.plain: Learning is usually explained by changes in how strongly brain cells connect to each other. In animals, though, learning also changes how easily individual neurons fire, and this study asks whether that happens in people. The researchers measured two indirect indices of how easily motor-cortex neurons fire, before and after motor training, using magnetic stimulation of the scalp.
summary.why: If confirmed, this would suggest that a second, cell-level mechanism (intrinsic plasticity) contributes to human motor learning alongside connection-strength changes, which matters for how we understand skill learning and recovery. The text does not show follow-up work or clinical applications, so these links remain speculative.

papers.abstract: Learning is commonly explained by changes in synaptic strength. In animals, however, learning also engages intrinsic plasticity -- changes in how readily neurons convert synaptic input into firing. Its contribution to human learning has been unclear, because conventional non-invasive measures of cortical excitability primarily reflect synaptic strength. Here we used controllable-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation to estimate two biophysical indices of intrinsic excitability in human motor cortex, before and after motor training. Training produced signatures of increased intrinsic excitability, selectively in the cortical representation of the trained muscle, but not an untrained muscle. Individuals showing larger intrinsic excitability changes learned faster, independently of changes in motor-evoked potential amplitude, an index of synaptic excitability that increased following training but did not predict learning rate. An axon model reproduced the measured changes through small shifts in membrane excitability. These findings provide evidence that intrinsic plasticity is expressed in the intact human brain, and that it represents a behaviourally relevant component of learning-related cortical adaptation.

papers.title: Universal barcoded connectomics for massively parallel single-neuron projection mapping in diverse vertebrate species
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767886 v1

summary.background:
- Connectomics: mapping which brain cells connect to which others.
- Projection mapping: following a neuron's long output fibres to their target regions.
- Barcoding: labelling each neuron with a unique short DNA sequence, delivered by a virus, so that sequencing the target tissue reveals which barcodes arrived where.
- Viral tropism: a virus's preference for infecting certain cell types; the paper addresses limits here that block the method in some species.
- HVC: a songbird brain region tied to song production, used here as a test system.
- Vertebrates: animals with a backbone, including fish, amphibians, birds, and mammals.
summary.one_liner: The paper reports sequencing-based barcoded connectomics, a method that tags individual neurons' projections with DNA barcodes, adapted to work across seven vertebrate species and validated by mapping thousands of songbird HVC neurons.
summary.plain: Scientists want to know which parts of the brain each nerve cell connects to, but good mapping tools exist mainly for a few lab animals. This paper adapts a DNA-barcoding approach so that it works in seven vertebrate species, from frogs and birds to non-human primates. The authors tested it by tracing the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, a brain region involved in birdsong, and found one set of reagents that worked across very different species.
summary.why: Being able to trace single neurons in many species at once could make it easier to compare brain wiring across animals, which is hard when each species needs its own tools. The text presents ready-to-use reagents and a framework for adapting them, but it does not show how far these results will carry to other brain regions or species.

papers.abstract: Neuroscience relies on diverse model species to understand animal behavior and brain function. Yet, tools for rapid, high-resolution brain connectivity mapping remain unavailable in most vertebrate species, slowing progress in many neuroscience models and rendering cross-species circuit comparisons challenging. Here, we overcome this barrier by establishing sequencing-based barcoded connectomics for rapid single-neuron tracing in seven vertebrate species ranging from frogs to birds to non-human primates. We develop a general solution to viral tropism and barcode trafficking, validate our reagents by mapping the projections of thousands of neurons in the songbird HVC, and discover a single set of reagents that functions across highly divergent species. Together, we provide ready-to-use barcoding reagents for diverse species and a simple framework for further adapting them if necessary, enabling high throughput single-neuron tracing across vertebrates.

papers.title: Adaptive behaviors emerge from Hebbian-like plasticity through flexible attractors
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767638 v1

summary.background:
- Hebbian learning: a rule where connections between neurons strengthen when they are active together, roughly "cells that fire together wire together."
- Local learning rule: an update that uses only information available at the connection itself, with no global reward signal.
- Closed-loop environment: the network's actions change what sensory input it receives next, which then feeds back into learning.
- Attractor: a stable pattern of activity a network settles into and tends to stay in; here, actions that produce input become self-sustaining.
- Probability matching: choosing options in proportion to how often they pay off, rather than always picking the best one.
- Heavy-tailed runs / Levy flights: movement patterns with many short steps and occasional very long ones, often seen in animal foraging.
- Reward optimization: the standard framing in which an agent is assumed to learn to maximize a reward value.
summary.one_liner: Simulated networks trained only with local Hebbian-like learning rules, with no reward objective and rewards delivered as ordinary sensory input, show reward-seeking features, with the prospective configuration rule matching the tested phenomena most consistently and behaviour explained by flexible attractors in activity-weight space.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether animals must be maximizing a reward to behave adaptively, or whether simple learning rules that strengthen connections between co-active neurons can produce similar behaviour. The authors built small networks, placed them in closed-loop environments where rewards appear as ordinary sensory input, and tested six standard learning rules. All of them learned to seek out the signal, but only one rule, prospective configuration, consistently reproduced the full set of tested behaviours.

papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior is commonly framed as an optimization problem, in which organisms learn to maximize reward. Here we show that simple networks with local, Hebbian-like learning rules, which have no reward objective, nonetheless reproduce hallmark features of animal reward-seeking when placed in closed-loop environments where rewards arrive as ordinary sensory input. Six canonical local learning rules were tested under these conditions, and despite most rules being designed for unsupervised representation learning, all rules learned to seek out signal. However, at the parameters tested, only one rule, prospective configuration, robustly captured all of a set of tested phenomena: reward-magnitude-dependent learning rates, probability matching, memory retention across contexts, and switching between exploration and exploitation with heavy-tailed statistics. In these networks, actions that produce input become self-sustaining states (attractors) of network dynamics. Attractors reside in an activity-weight space and mediate behaviors, and adapt to their environments rather than being fixed properties of the networks. These flexible geometries provide a parsimonious account of how heavy-tailed runs of repeated choices, which resemble Levy flights seen in foraging, also change with the environment. A single framework then makes predictions about behavior and neural population geometries that can be used to investigate the learning dynamics of the brain.

papers.title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767508 v1

summary.background:
- EEG: recording electrical activity of the brain through electrodes on the scalp; it is non-invasive but coarse in space.
- Population coding: the idea that information is carried by the joint activity of many neurons tuned to different features (here, orientation), not by one neuron alone.
- Encoding-decoding framework: a model is fit to predict brain signals from a stimulus, then inverted to estimate the stimulus or the tuned responses from new brain data.
- Correlated variability (noise correlations): trial-to-trial fluctuations that neurons share; when they are similar in tuning, they can limit how precisely a population encodes information.
- Alpha power: strength of roughly 8–12 Hz rhythmic EEG activity, often linked to cortical idling or gating.
- Pupil dilation: a non-invasive index of arousal and neuromodulatory state (e.g., noradrenergic activity).
- Working memory: holding information briefly in mind for later use.
summary.one_liner: Using EEG with an encoding-decoding approach, this paper reconstructs orientation-tuned population responses in humans and shows that moment-to-moment representational precision tracks correlated variability between decoded channels, prestimulus alpha power, and pupil size.
summary.plain: The brain's internal picture of what we see gets sharper or blurrier from moment to moment, and this affects how well we perceive and remember things. The authors recorded brain activity with EEG (electrodes on the scalp) while people viewed and remembered orientations, then used a statistical decoding method to reconstruct how groups of neurons were responding over time. They found that the sharpness of this internal picture predicted later memory performance, and that it was linked to a particular pattern of shared noise among similar neural channels and to two easily measured signals: alpha brain rhythms before a stimulus and pupil size.
summary.why: The work offers candidate mechanisms and non-invasive markers (alpha power, pupil size) for how precise sensory representations are, which could be useful for studying attention, memory and brain state in humans. The text does not show how far these markers generalise beyond this task, so their wider value remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.

papers.title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767170 v1

summary.background:
- Audiomotor circuit: brain areas linking hearing to movement.
- Neural population activity: the joint firing pattern of many neurons, analyzed as a single trajectory or shape.
- Manifold: a low-dimensional shape that population activity traces out; here described as cone-shaped.
- Interstimulus interval: the time gap between successive metronome clicks.
- Pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA): a frontal cortex region involved in planning and timing movements.
- Tempo: the speed of the beat.
- Synchronization-continuation tapping: tapping in time with a beat and then keeping the rhythm after the sound stops.
summary.one_liner: Recordings from 4,719 neurons across six nodes of the monkey audiomotor circuit show that the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) carries a population-level, cone-shaped timing manifold that encodes tempo, produced interval, and tap phase during beat-synchronized tapping.
summary.plain: Humans can tap along to a musical beat, but how the brain builds the internal sense of that beat is not well understood. The researchers recorded activity from thousands of nerve cells in monkeys tapping in time with metronomes at different speeds, and compared several brain regions involved in hearing and movement.
summary.why: The paper argues that a specific frontal region, preSMA, holds a hierarchical timing signal that sits above auditory and motor areas, which could help explain how rhythm guides movement. The text reports these findings from one study, so how well they generalize to other animals or to human timing is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.

papers.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.765917 v1

summary.background:
- fMRI: a brain scanner that tracks blood flow as a proxy for neural activity, so it shows which regions are active, not direct signals.
- Intrinsic motivation: doing something for its own sake, not for an external reward.
- Wanting vs. liking: two proposed dimensions of motivation, the drive to close an information gap versus the pleasure of the content itself.
- Intersubject neural similarity: how similar brain activity is across different people watching the same material; a sign of shared processing.
- Default mode network: a set of brain regions often active during internal thought and not focused on an external task.
- Retrospective ratings: participants reported their feelings after the fact, which can be affected by memory.
summary.one_liner: An fMRI study of free internet browsing that separates self-reported "wanting" (wanting to resolve an information gap) from "liking" (enjoying the information), and links each to browsing stability, brain activity, and later recall, compared with passive viewing of the same content.
summary.plain: People often look things up or read online without any outside reward, simply because they are curious. This study put volunteers in a brain scanner while they browsed the internet freely, then asked them to recall what they had looked at and rate, moment by moment, how much they wanted the information and how much they enjoyed it. The authors report that both ratings tracked steadier browsing and different brain systems, and that wanting helped memory mainly when enjoyment was low.
summary.why: It moves the study of curiosity from simple lab tasks toward self-directed behaviour in a realistic setting, which may matter for understanding learning and attention online. The text does not show how far the findings generalise beyond this sample and setup, so their broader significance is still uncertain.

papers.abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

papers.title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767044 v1

summary.background:
- Additional-singleton search task: finding a target among items where one item is a salient, task-irrelevant distractor.
- Statistical learning of distractor locations: attention can become biased away from a spot where distractors often appear, without awareness.
- Egocentric (viewer-centered) coding: locations described relative to the observer's current position or view.
- Allocentric (world-centered) coding: locations described relative to the external environment, independent of the observer's view.
- Prior work found target locations can be learned in world-centered coordinates, but distractor locations seem tied to the viewpoint.
- Contextual anchors: stable landmarks that help define a spatial layout.
- Explicit knowledge: the participant is told about the regularity, as opposed to learning it implicitly.
summary.one_liner: Across two experiments in a tabletop additional-singleton search task where observers moved around the table, learned suppression of a high-probability distractor failed to follow the fixed external location even with embedded contextual anchors and explicit instruction, supporting viewer-centered spatial coding for distractor learning.
summary.plain: The study asks whether people can learn where a distracting item is likely to appear in a way that stays correct as they walk around a table. Participants searched a display on a table while changing their standing position, and the distractor stayed in a fixed spot in the room. The authors report that people did not learn the distractor's room-based location, even when landmarks were built into the display and participants were told about the pattern.
summary.why: It suggests that ignoring distractions may be tied to the viewpoint a person is currently in, which is a useful constraint for theories of attention and spatial memory. The text does not show how far these findings extend beyond this set-up, so the broader implications remain uncertain.

papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer's current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Together with previous findings showing robust egocentric distractor-location learning using the same set-up, these findings strengthen the view that learned distractor suppression relies primarily on viewer-centered spatial coding, potentially reflecting a process linked to viewpoint-specific action selection.

papers.title: Identifying aligned tensor decompositions across heterogeneous neural datasets
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766278 v1

summary.background:
- Neural recordings: measurements of activity from many neurons over time, often across repeated trials of a task.
- Tensor decomposition: a way of splitting a multi-dimensional data array (e.g., neurons x time x trials) into a small number of components, each a pattern plus how strongly it appears in each dimension.
- Alignment: matching up data from different sessions or animals when the recorded cells are not the same ones.
- Optogenetic inhibition: switching off a brain region with light in genetically modified animals, to test what that region contributes.
- ALM (anterior lateral motor cortex): a mouse frontal region involved in planning movements such as licking choices.
- Label-free: the method does not use task labels (e.g., reach direction or choice) during fitting; labels are only used afterwards for interpretation.
summary.one_liner: Neuralign is a tensor-decomposition method that jointly aligns and factorises heterogeneous neural recordings into shared temporal components linked to individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, trials, or behavioural labels.
summary.plain: Modern brain recordings come from many sessions, brain areas and animals, and the recorded cells differ each time, so it is hard to see patterns they share. This paper presents a method that lines these different recordings up and splits them into shared building blocks, each showing a common activity pattern and how strongly it appears in each trial and each neuron. The authors report tests on simulated data, artificial recurrent networks, monkey motor-cortex data, and 93 mouse brain-wide recordings.
summary.why: Combining recordings that do not share the same cells or trials could make large public datasets easier to compare and interpret. The text reports that one component isolated the response to silencing a motor-planning region (ALM) in mice, and that a reference from correct trials revealed inhibition-related activity on error trials; the wider significance for neuroscience is not established by this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

papers.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766497 v1

summary.background:
- Neural population activity: recordings from many neurons at once, treated as a point moving through a high-dimensional space.
- Spike-train co-smoothing: predicting the activity of held-out neurons from the others, a standard benchmark task (Neural Latents Benchmark, NLB'21).
- Hyperbolic geometry: a curved space, in which tree-like or hierarchical structures are often represented more compactly than in flat space; the Poincaré ball is one model of it.
- Curvature: a number describing how strongly a space bends; positive curvature here means the Poincaré-ball model is in use with a learned scale parameter.
- State space model (S4D): a sequence model that processes time series using a set of decaying oscillatory components.
- Ring manifold: a loop-shaped pattern of population activity, often linked to motor circuits.
- Self-supervised masked prediction: training by hiding parts of the data and asking the model to fill them in.
summary.one_liner: NeuroMASS v4 is a neural network for predicting held-out spike activity on Neural Latents Benchmark recordings that embeds neural population states in a learnable hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) space and claims the learned curvature tracks circuit topology across motor and cognitive cortical datasets.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether the shape of the space that brain activity lives in can be learned from recordings of many neurons firing in monkeys. The authors build a model that takes spike counts from many neurons, predicts the missing parts of them, and learns a curved "hyperbolic" geometry along the way. They report that the learned curvature is clearly positive for two motor datasets and near zero for a frontal cognitive dataset, and they interpret this as a sign of the circuit's underlying structure.
summary.why: If learned geometry really reflects circuit organization, it could give a compact, comparable way to describe different brain areas. However, the text gives only a summary of the claim; it does not show the statistical tests, baselines, or controls behind "statistically predicts," so the strength of the evidence is hard to judge from this description alone.

papers.abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.
